Photograph: Jens Schlueter/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle airport on the day of the drone attack. Photograph: Jens Schlueter/Getty Images Germany Germany blames Russia for drone attack at Leipzig airport Government says ‘dangerous behaviour’ is part of effort by Moscow to cause damage with hybrid attacks Kate Connolly in Berlin Tue 1 Sep 2026 14.01 EDT Last modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 16.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The German government has blamed Russia for the drone attack on Leipzig airport last month, calling it “dangerous behaviour” and part of a systematic and concerted effort by Moscow to “cause great damage” through a large number of hybrid attacks. The interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, and the foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, ended weeks of speculation and the government’s hesitancy to blame Russia, saying in a brisk 10-minute briefing in Berlin that all indications were the Russian state had provided the knowhow and equipment for the planned attack and “low-level agents” were recruited to carry it out. A drone loaded with explosives was discovered at Leipzig/Halle airport on 4 August attached to the wing of a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane used to transport weapons to Ukraine. It failed to detonate but could have caused a catastrophe, authorities said. Russia will face a package of penalty measures, Wadephul said, adding that the German government saw “a need for appropriate and necessary action in this situation”. It would respond “to this hybrid attack in Leipzig with proportionate and measured, yet equally resolute, action”, he said. “We are not at war, but we are a daily target of hybrid warfare.” He added: “The dangerous behaviour of the Russian Federation is part of attempts at destabilisation, disinformation, threats, sabotage and aggression.” Berlin regretted the abysmal state of its relations with Moscow, he said. View image in fullscreen Germany’s foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, said Germany was ‘a daily target of hybrid warfare’. Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/Shutterstock The EU expressed “full solidarity” with Germany over the attack, and Nato assured Berlin that it would defend its members. The Russian ambassador had been summoned to the foreign ministry at that very moment to be informed of the consequences, Wadephul said. The Russian consulate in Bonn will be closed later this month, and Russian House, a sprawling cultural and science institute in the centre of Berlin, which is alleged to house Russian spies and to have been the launchpad for a number of hybrid attacks carried out in Germany over the past few years, is to be turned out of its rented building. A clampdown on Russia’s shadow fleet – illegal ships carrying Russian oil and other supplies in the Baltic and North seas – is also planned. Sweden and Finland track and disrupt the shadow fleet but Germany does not, so vessels regularly opt to sail via German waters in its foreign economic zones. New lists of people on a blacklist would be drawn up and tighter border controls of Russians entering Germany would be carried out, Wadephul said. Parallel to these moves, Berlin is also backing the European Commission’s 22nd package of sanctions, to cover a further 1,600 companies and organisations with a Russian connection. Responding to ​Germany’s announcement, ‌Russia’s foreign ministry ​spokesperson, ​Maria Zakharova, said Moscow would respond to what she called Berlin’s “anti-Russian action”, according to the Interfax news agency. The government has previously said it does not intend to directly involve Nato by invoking article 4 of the alliance. However, its Nato and European partners were informed about the investigation and agreed on the planned consequences, Wadephul confirmed. The Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, promised “full solidarity” with Berlin. Rutte said Berlin had put forward clear evidence of Moscow’s role in the “hybrid attack” and welcomed the measures announced in response, while von der Leyen vowed to “keep the EU united despite these escalating and serious acts”. View image in fullscreen Police officers searching for evidence at Leipzig/Halle airport in August. Photograph: Sebastian Willnow/DPA/AP Tuesday’s announcement marks the first time the German government has concretely named Russia as responsible for the attack. It marks the lowest point in decades for relations between Russia and the EU’s largest member, which had already plunged after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. This weekend will see a critical election in the eastern states of Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg Vorpommern, in which the war in Ukraine and relations with Russia have been a focal point. The far-right populist Alternative für Deutschland, which is pushing a pro-Russia agenda as it seeks to win an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt, has accused the government of double standards over its treatment of Russia. Urging the government to prove Russia’s involvement in the Leipzig incident earlier this week, it said the same rigour should be applied to investigations into the attack on the Nord Stream pipeline, for which Ukraine is alleged to have been responsible. View image in fullscreen Freight by an Ukrainian Antonov plane at Leipzig/Halle airport filmed a day after a drone was spotted nearby. Photograph: NEWS5/AFP/Getty Images The drone in the Leipzig incident was carrying 600g of explosives and was discovered in the security area of ​​the airport close to Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes on the night of 4-5 August. The explosive device detonator appeared to have failed. A second drone was believed to have been part of the planned attack but investigators have since thrown doubt on that theory. Traces of the military explosive hexogen were found on the edge of the airport on 14 August along with a further drone, investigators confirmed. Had the devices exploded they could have caused a catastrophe, German officials said. The chancellor, Friedrich Merz, who last week said whoever was behind the attack “will pay”, did not attend the briefing to the press and public on Tuesday. Konstantin von Notz, the Green party’s security policy expert and commissioner for intelligence oversight, criticised the government before the announcement for what he described as its failure to stand up to Vladimir Putin in the face of the growing hybrid threat from Russia. “The federal government must finally stop being hesitant, reticent and timid. Things must be called by their name, and decisive action must be taken,” he said in an interview with the RND network. Even within his own Christian Democratic Union party, Merz has faced calls to be tougher towards Russia. On Tuesday, the party’s foreign policy expert, Roderich Kiesewetter, urged the chancellor to take a tougher line against Russia, accusing successive governments of exercising “extreme caution with regard to Russian state terrorism on German soil”. Citing sources in German intelligence, Bild Zeitung said direct connections had been made by investigators between other drone and explosives finds and incidents in Germany and across Europe, including in Romania, Italy, Poland, Bulgaria and the UK. A cache of weapons discovered recently in a Berlin forest are thought to be connected to Russian activities in Romania. Investigators in various countries are believed to be working in parallel with each other. Photograph: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty Images Washington DC Virginia and DC sue to stop Trump’s arch as government looks to start construction Legal challenges to Donald Trump’s proposed memorial arch are mounting even as its construction is imminent Associated Press Sat 31 Oct 2026 13.57 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The legal challenges to Donald Trump ’s proposed memorial arch are mounting, with the District of Columbia and Virginia suing in federal court on Saturday as the administration says construction could begin as early as next week. There are now three lawsuits calling for a halt to potential work on a monument that would rise 250ft (76 meters) on a patch of grass off the bridge that spans the Potomac River, connecting the city with the Arlington national cemetery. That would make the arch 100ft taller (30 meters) than the Statue of Liberty is from its base to the top of the torch. The US district judge Tanya Chutkan is already considering issuing an order to halt the project until the original lawsuit against the Trump administration by three Vietnam war veterans and an architectural historian is resolved. She held a hearing on Friday but did not immediately act, though she said she would move expeditiously. Trump plans to begin DC golf course renovation in defiance of judge’s order Read more In the latest lawsuit, two attorneys general, Brian Schwalb of Washington DC and Jay Jones of Virginia, argue that “as soon as defendants break ground on this project, they will inflict irreparable harm on both the District and Virginia. The arch site sits at the center of a major traffic artery between the District and Virginia, in the monumental core of the capital, on an island that straddles the Potomac River. During the three-year period of construction, the arch project will inevitably snarl traffic between the jurisdictions, produce pollution and storm water runoff in the Potomac, interfere with emergency services, and pose numerous other challenges.” As the original plaintiffs have, they also are seeking a temporary restraining order that would slow the administration’s plans to move ahead imminently with construction. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The lawsuit raises concerns about how the traffic interruption would affect emergency responses in a region where joint operations are the norm, and where a January 2025 midair collision between a US military helicopter and passenger airliner killed 67 people. The Republican administration, in a recent court filing, said it had plans to seek final approval of the project, a Trump favorite, at Thursday’s meeting of the Capital National Planning Commission and possibly begin construction the same day, despite the two pending lawsuits. On Friday, the government submitted a 106-page plan for the arch that envisions a massive structure more than 12 stories high that includes a huge bronze statue of Lady Liberty with wings and carrying a torch with an eternal flame. The structure would include an observation deck with views to the east and west, an “occupied roof” and two mezzanines. Inside the arch are rooms for program space, offices, a staff lounge, circular staircases, multiple elevators and a “fire command center”. The project proposes significant traffic changes in the area, including rerouting traffic on nearby roads. Administration officials have said the arch also will have a national security function.
